title: AWS Parameter Store Alternatives: 6 Options When You Need Rotation and Scale
summary: What to use when AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store runs out of room, from missing rotation to read throttling and size caps, and what each option takes to run.
body_markdown:
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store is the path of least resistance on AWS: standard parameters are free, and Lambda, ECS, and CloudFormation read them natively. The trouble starts once more of the stack depends on it:


- a release rolls out dozens of services and runs into rate limits, because they all fetch their parameters in the same second
- a database password hasn't changed since the day it was created because Parameter Store can't rotate it


Parameter Store stores values, which makes it suboptimal for managing application secrets that need frequent rotation or go beyond AWS.


Teams often move beyond Parameter Store when manual caching and retry logic, Lambda functions, and the split with AWS Secrets Manager become too annoying.


Most of those teams land on a dedicated secrets manager such as Infisical, which offers much more comprehensive secrets management while syncing values into Parameter Store, so services can keep reading parameters from Parameter Store.


## How the SSM Parameter Store alternatives compare

## 1. Infisical


Infisical offers an open-source secrets manager. Teams moving from Parameter Store usually centralize credentials in Infisical and inject them directly into each process’s runtime. Infisical automatically rotates credentials so you no longer need Lambda functions to rotate credentials.


Infisical offers a[Parameter Store sync](https://infisical.com/docs/integrations/secret-syncs/aws-parameter-store) that can import your existing parameters and then push values from Infisical into Parameter Store.


Any Lambda functions, ECS task definitions, and CloudFormation templates keep working while Infisical becomes the source of truth for any secrets, whether on AWS or not. Infisical runs as Infisical Cloud or self-hosted, air-gapped included, and its core is MIT-licensed.


**Best for:** AWS teams that started on Parameter Store and now need rotation, environment separation, and one place for the secrets that live outside AWS.


**Strengths:**


- One dashboard shows dev, staging, and prod side by side, with folders, references between secrets, and search across values, so finding a setting doesn't mean walking parameter paths in the AWS console.
- [Secret rotation](https://infisical.com/docs/documentation/platform/secret-rotation/overview) for 30+ targets, including OpenAI, Stripe, Okta, Auth0, AWS IAM, Azure and GCP credentials, LDAP, and databases from PostgreSQL and MySQL to MSSQL, Oracle, MongoDB, and Redis.
- Dynamic secrets for 30+ targets, so a workload can request a short-lived credential for a database, AWS IAM, GCP IAM, Azure Entra ID, Kubernetes, SSH, LDAP, or Kafka that expires on its own.
- Beyond Parameter Store, syncs reach 50+ destinations, among them Secrets Manager, Terraform Cloud, Vercel, GitLab, GitHub, and the Azure and Google Cloud secret stores.
- The Infisical Agent runs as an ECS sidecar, and Kubernetes gets an operator, a CSI driver, and an injector.
- Changes to sensitive environments can require sign-off, people can request temporary access, and every environment keeps versions with point-in-time recovery.
- AWS workloads authenticate using the IAM role they already have (AWS Auth), so no new credential has to be handed to a service to reach Infisical.


**How it improves on AWS Parameter Store:**


- Credentials rotate where they're stored, so configuration and the credentials that change no longer live in two different AWS services.
- Services that read from Infisical directly, through the agent, an SDK, or the Kubernetes operator, stop drawing on Parameter Store's shared read quota, so a parallel rollout doesn't queue behind throttled Get calls.
- A changed value reaches running workloads. The agent in an[ECS task](https://infisical.com/docs/integrations/platforms/ecs-with-agent) checks for changes on an interval and can run a reload command, and the Kubernetes operator can restart a deployment when its secrets change.
- Environments are part of the model rather than a` /prod/` and` /staging/` naming convention that every team has to follow by hand.


**Pricing model:** free and paid plans on Infisical Cloud, and a free open-source core to self-host, with paid enterprise features under a commercial license.


## 2. AWS Secrets Manager


[AWS Secrets Manager](https://infisical.com/blog/aws-secrets-manager-complete-guide) is AWS's managed service for credentials, API keys, and other secrets, with a few rotation templates built in. AWS itself recommends it for credentials that need rotation.


If you use Parameter Store, Secrets Manager is an easy migration because it shares the same IAM, console, and AWS services reading it.


AWS Secrets Manager is a solid choice for any organization exclusively using AWS. But it only rotates RDS, Aurora, DocumentDB, and Redshift credentials without a function. Anything else rotates through a Lambda function you have to write and maintain.


AWS Secrets Manager isn’t free, either. It bills per secret per month, with every environment, account, and Region holding its own billed copy. It’s best for teams that don’t mind maintaining the Lambda functions and who don’t plan to move beyond AWS.


**Best for:** AWS-only teams whose credentials need rotating and are mostly RDS, Aurora, DocumentDB, or Redshift.


**Strengths:**


- Managed rotation for Aurora, RDS, DocumentDB, and Redshift admin credentials, with no Lambda to write.
- Managed external secrets rotate partner credentials such as Datadog, GitLab, MongoDB Atlas, Snowflake, Salesforce, and Twilio.
- IAM identity and resource policies, attribute-based access control, and cross-account sharing.
- Replication to other AWS Regions, and high API limits.


**Limitations:**


- A credential outside the supported list requires a Lambda function you need to write, wire up, and monitor per secret type.
- Secrets Manager has no environments, so teams separate them with naming schemes, IAM policies, or separate accounts.
- Replication stays inside AWS. Secrets for another cloud, a CI/CD system, or on-premises need tooling of your own.
- No approval workflow on secret changes and no dynamic secrets.


**Pricing model:** per secret per month plus per 10,000 API calls, with each cross-Region replica billed as its own secret.


## 3. Doppler


Doppler is a hosted platform for app secrets and configuration, organized into projects, environments, and configs, and reached through a dashboard, CLI, API, syncs, and a Kubernetes operator.


**Best for:** small and mid-size product teams that want a hosted home for environment variables and app config, with nothing to run.


**Strengths:**


- Projects, environments, and configs, where one config can inherit from another.
- Syncs into many clouds, CI/CD systems, and hosting platforms.
- Every secret keeps its versions, can be rolled back, and has its own access log, and changes can go through change requests.
- A Kubernetes operator.


**Limitations:**


- It's closed source, and self-hosting is Enterprise only.
- Documented rotation covers AWS targets (Secrets Manager, Postgres on AWS, and IAM users) and GCP service account keys. Other targets need a rotation integration of your own.
- Dynamic secrets need Enterprise and are documented for two targets, AWS IAM and Azure service principals.


**Pricing model:** per user per month across tiers, with add-ons priced per seat.


## 4. HashiCorp Vault


HashiCorp Vault manages secrets and encryption keys, either self-managed or as the managed HCP Vault Dedicated. Its license changed from MPL to the Business Source License in August 2023, and IBM completed its acquisition of HashiCorp in February 2025.


Vault is a powerful secrets management platform, but separate infrastructure rather than a product. There’s a reason many large companies have multiple engineers that exclusively work on Vault. Running Vault means:


- Running a cluster you need to seal and unseal on restart
- Hosting a storage backend
- Ensuring high availability because secrets are mission-critical
- Upgrade planning for new versions
- Learning HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL) to write policies


Vault is highly configurable and capable, but complex to maintain. It suits organizations with a platform team ready to run it as an internal service (or the ability to hire a team).


**Best for:** organizations with a platform team that can staff a central secrets and encryption service.


**Strengths:**


- Many secrets engines, covering a wide range of credential types.
- Database and AWS IAM credentials issued on demand, tracked by lease, and revocable.
- The transit engine, which encrypts and decrypts application data without giving the application the keys.
- Policies scoped by path, with templating, which will feel familiar to anyone who scoped IAM to parameter paths.
- Three Kubernetes routes: its own operator, a CSI provider, and a sidecar injector.


**Limitations:**


- Running it yourself means a cluster to operate and staff who know Vault. With HCP Vault Dedicated, HashiCorp operates it and bills by the hour.
- There's no environment object. Mounts, paths, and policies give it structure, and each team designs its own layout.
- Approvals, namespaces, and Secrets Sync to cloud stores are Enterprise features.
- The Business Source License isn't an open-source license, which means legal review for anyone embedding or offering Vault.


**Pricing model:** Community costs nothing under BSL terms, Enterprise is sold through sales with no published prices, and HCP Vault Dedicated charges per cluster hour, with a per-client charge on some tiers.


## 5. OpenBao


OpenBao forked Vault after HashiCorp's 2023 license change. It's an OpenSSF Sandbox project under the Linux Foundation and keeps Vault's API and operating model, licensed MPL-2.0.


It offers similar ergonomics to Vault, but this fork doesn’t share all of Vault’s features and can’t offer vendor support as it’s a pure open-source project. OpenBao is great for teams who have experience with Vault, but need more customization.


**Best for:** Vault users who want an OSI license and community governance, and who are comfortable running their own clusters.


**Strengths:**


- MPL-2.0, with documented open governance.
- Namespaces, plus control groups for approvals, are part of the free project, where Vault reserves both for Enterprise.
- Engines carried over from Vault: KV, databases, SSH, transit, Kubernetes, LDAP, and PKI with ACME.
- No license fee, and frequent releases.


**Limitations:**


- The fork dropped the cloud secrets engines and the cloud IAM auth methods, so an ECS task or Lambda function can't sign in with its IAM role, and dynamic AWS credentials need a plugin you write.
- Dynamic database credentials work for five engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, Cassandra, InfluxDB, and Valkey.
- Vault's operating model comes along unchanged: a cluster to run, unseal, upgrade, and staff.
- No managed service, vendor support contract, or sync to Parameter Store or any other store.


**Pricing model:** free.


## 6. SOPS


SOPS is a command-line tool that encrypts secret values inside YAML, JSON, ENV, and INI files so they can be committed to Git.


This is different from a secrets manager, which injects secrets at runtime so they can never end up in Git. SOPS is free and doesn’t run as a separate service. It does require managing encryption keys and constant encryption and decryption operations.


**Best for:** GitOps teams that keep configuration in Git and want file-level encryption with keys they already hold, including AWS KMS keys.


**Strengths:**


- Encrypts values and leaves keys readable, so encrypted files still produce meaningful diffs in review.
- Supports AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, age, PGP, and Vault or OpenBao transit as key sources.
- Nothing to run, and no service to call at deploy time.
- Key groups split decryption across several keys.


**Limitations:**


- It encrypts files and doesn't serve them: no API, dashboard, rotation, dynamic secrets, or syncs, so every pipeline scripts its own decrypt step.
- Whoever holds a key has access. Removing someone means re-keying the files and rotating the secret values by hand.
- Requires managing encryption keys.
- Requires frequent encryption and decryption operations.
- There's no audit log or approval step of its own. Git history, pull-request review, and KMS logs stand in.


**Pricing model:** free. The key backend, such as AWS KMS, bills separately.


## Moving off AWS Parameter Store


If you move to Infisical from AWS Parameter Store, create an AWS connection and add a Parameter Store sync to import secrets.


Infisical pulls in existing parameters and then writes changes back to the same path. Services keep reading their parameters as before. Move the ones that hit throttling, or that need changes without a redeploy, to read from Infisical directly, then switch on rotation for the credentials. Our roundup of the[best secrets management tools](https://infisical.com/blog/best-secret-management-tools) covers options beyond AWS.


## FAQ


### What are the alternatives to AWS Parameter Store?


Most teams that outgrow AWS Parameter Store move to a secrets manager like Infisical. It suits AWS teams that need to rotate credentials, see environments kept side by side, and manage secrets from outside AWS in one place. It also syncs back into Parameter Store so the services that read parameters keep working.


### Is AWS SSM Parameter Store free?


Standard parameters in AWS SSM Parameter Store are free, including reads at the default throughput. Advanced parameters carry a monthly fee each, and throughput above the default is charged per 10,000 interactions. A standard parameter holds up to 4 KB, with up to 10,000 per Region, and advanced parameters raise those limits to 8 KB and 100,000.


### What is AWS Parameter Store used for?


AWS Parameter Store holds application configuration, such as hostnames, feature settings, and connection strings, and low-risk secrets stored as KMS-encrypted SecureString parameters.


### Why use Secrets Manager instead of Parameter Store?


Use AWS Secrets Manager instead of Parameter Store when a credential has to rotate. Parameter Store has no rotation, and AWS recommends Secrets Manager for credentials. Secrets Manager bills per secret where standard parameters are free, so many teams keep configuration in Parameter Store and credentials in Secrets Manager.


### What is the difference between AWS AppConfig and Parameter Store?


AWS AppConfig controls how configuration changes are rolled out, while Parameter Store stores the values.
